[Textbook misprint: the structure printed for dopamine (a) is defective. Its side chain is drawn as three \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) groups ending in a free valence with nothing attached, so as printed the molecule has no functional group other than the two phenolic hydroxyls. Dopamine is 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzene-1,2-diol : the side chain should be \(\mathrm{-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2}\), one carbon shorter and ending in a primary amine. The answer above lists what the printed structure shows and names the missing group. Separately, the structure printed for thyroxine (b) carries only two iodine atoms where the real hormone carries four, two on each ring; that does not change the set of functional groups the question asks for.]

[Textbook note (not an error): part (c) has no unambiguous answer at the level this chapter develops. The chapter teaches that a halogen exerts a -I effect, which destabilises a carbocation and makes \(\mathrm{\overset{\oplus}{C}H_3}\) the most stable of the three — the answer given, and the one that makes part (c) the exact mirror of part (b). The same chapter also teaches that a halogen has lone pairs and can show a +R effect, which acting alone would stabilise a chlorine-bearing carbocation and reverse the order. The chapter never weighs the two effects against each other for a halogen bonded directly to the positive carbon.]

[Textbook misprint: the formula is printed as \(\mathrm{CH_3CHCHCH_3}\), with no bond shown between the two middle carbons. As printed each of them has only three bonds, so the formula is not a valid structure and none of the four alternatives can apply to it. The intended compound is but-2-ene, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3}\), which is how the question is answered above. The stem is reproduced exactly as printed.]
